questionText: Find the average of: 44, 26, 51, 56, 48
hints: Average = Sum of all numbers ÷ Count of numbers.
Add up all 5 numbers first.
Then divide the total by 5.

misconceptions.A: Remember: Average = Total ÷ Count. Recheck your total and count.
misconceptions.B: Correct! The answer is 45.
misconceptions.C: Remember: Average = Total ÷ Count. Recheck your total and count.
misconceptions.D: Remember: Average = Total ÷ Count. Recheck your total and count.

questionText: The average of 4 numbers is 58. If 3 of the numbers are 71, 56, 72, find the missing number.
hints: First find the total: Average × Number of items.
Then subtract the known numbers from the total.
Total should be 58 × 4 = 232.

misconceptions.A: Correct! The answer is 33.
misconceptions.B: Remember: Average = Total ÷ Count. Recheck your total and count.
misconceptions.C: Remember: Average = Total ÷ Count. Recheck your total and count.
misconceptions.D: Remember: Average = Total ÷ Count. Recheck your total and count.

questionText: The average of 4 numbers is 49. When a new number 59 is added, what is the new average?
hints: Find the old total first: 49 × 4.
Add 59 to get the new total.
Divide new total by 5 (the new count).

misconceptions.A: Correct! The answer is 51.
misconceptions.B: Remember: Average = Total ÷ Count. Recheck your total and count.
misconceptions.C: Remember: Average = Total ÷ Count. Recheck your total and count.
misconceptions.D: Remember: Average = Total ÷ Count. Recheck your total and count.

questionText: Rohit's runs in five cricket matches were: Match 1 34, Match 2 52, Match 3 47, Match 4 25, Match 5 43. In which match did he score the most runs?
hints: This asks you to find the biggest number in a list and say which match it belongs to.
Compare the tens digits of the five scores first. Which scores have the biggest tens digit?
Example: Scores of Game 1 18, Game 2 31, Game 3 27. The biggest number is 31, so the most runs came in Game 2.

stepByStep.text: Look at the tens digits: 34, 52, 47, 25 and 43 have tens digits 3, 5, 4, 2 and 4.
The biggest tens digit is 5, so 52 is the biggest score.
52 runs were scored in Match 2, so the answer is Match 2.

misconceptions.A: Match 3 has 47 runs, which is the second biggest score. Check whether any score is in the fifties.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 52 is bigger than 34, 47, 25 and 43, and it belongs to Match 2.
misconceptions.C: Match 5 has 43 runs. Compare it with 52 and 47 to see which is biggest.
misconceptions.D: Match 4 has 25 runs, which is the smallest score. The question asks for the most runs, so look for the biggest number.

questionText: In a pictograph, each picture of a book stands for 5 books sold. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday has 6 pictures, Wednesday has 3 pictures and Thursday has 5 pictures. On which day were the fewest books sold?
hints: Every picture stands for the same number of books, so think about what the number of pictures tells you.
The day with the fewest pictures has the fewest books. Compare 4, 6, 3 and 5.
Example: Each picture stands for 2 kites. Ravi has 7 pictures, Sita has 2 pictures and Anu has 5 pictures. Sita has the fewest pictures, so Sita has the fewest kites.

stepByStep.text: Each picture stands for the same number of books, so fewer pictures means fewer books.
The numbers of pictures are 4, 6, 3 and 5. The smallest is 3.
Wednesday has 3 pictures, which is 15 books.
The fewest books were sold on Wednesday.

misconceptions.A: Monday has 4 pictures, which is 20 books. Is there a day with fewer pictures than 4?
misconceptions.B: Tuesday has 6 pictures, the most of all. The question asks for the fewest, so look for the smallest number of pictures.
misconceptions.C: Thursday has 5 pictures, which is 25 books. Look for a day with fewer pictures.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Wednesday has only 3 pictures, fewer than any other day, so it has the fewest books.

questionText: In a tally chart, each bundle stands for 5 and each single stroke stands for 1. The row for parrots has 3 bundles and 2 single strokes. How many parrots were counted?
hints: A tally chart counts in fives. Work out the bundles first, then add the single strokes.
Find how many the 3 bundles stand for by multiplying 3 by 5.
Example: 2 bundles and 4 single strokes. The bundles give 2 x 5 = 10, and 10 + 4 = 14.

stepByStep.text: Each bundle stands for 5, so 3 bundles stand for 15.

misconceptions.A: Great counting! 3 bundles make 15, and 2 more strokes make 17.
misconceptions.B: This adds 3 and 2 as if every mark stood for 1. Remember that each bundle stands for 5.
misconceptions.C: This counts the 3 bundles but leaves out the 2 single strokes. Add them on.
misconceptions.D: This writes the 3 and the 2 side by side. Each bundle is worth 5, so multiply 3 by 5 and then add 2.

questionText: The number of children present in Class 4 was: Mon 38, Tue 35, Wed 40, Thu 32. How many more children were present on Wednesday than on Tuesday?
hints: The words 'how many more' ask you to compare two numbers from the list.
Pick out the numbers for Wednesday and Tuesday only. They are 40 and 35.
Example: Mon 26, Tue 19. To find how many more on Monday, subtract: 26 - 19 = 7.

stepByStep.text: Wednesday has 40 children and Tuesday has 35 children.
Subtract to find how many more.
5 more children were present on Wednesday.

misconceptions.A: This adds 40 and 35. To find how many more, subtract the smaller number from the bigger one.
misconceptions.B: This compares Wednesday with Thursday. The question asks about Wednesday and Tuesday.
misconceptions.C: That is right! 40 - 35 = 5, so 5 more children came on Wednesday.
misconceptions.D: This compares Monday with Tuesday. Use Wednesday's number, 40, and Tuesday's number, 35.

questionText: A bar graph shows the samosas sold at a stall: Monday 12, Tuesday 15, Wednesday 9, Thursday 15, Friday 11. Which two days have bars of the same height?
hints: Bars of the same height show the same number. Look for a number that appears twice.
Read the five numbers one by one: 12, 15, 9, 15, 11. Which number do you see two times?
Example: Red 7, Blue 4, Green 7, Yellow 6. The number 7 appears twice, so the bars for Red and Green are equally tall.

stepByStep.text: Bars are equally tall when their numbers are equal.
In the list 12, 15, 9, 15, 11 only the number 15 appears twice.
15 belongs to Tuesday and Thursday, so the equal bars are Tuesday and Thursday.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Both Tuesday and Thursday show 15 samosas, so their bars are the same height.
misconceptions.B: Monday shows 12 and Friday shows 11. They are close, but not equal. Look for two numbers that match exactly.
misconceptions.C: Monday shows 12 and Thursday shows 15. Find the other day that also shows 15.
misconceptions.D: Wednesday shows 9 and Friday shows 11. Look for two days with exactly the same number.

questionText: The children of Class 4 each chose one favourite fruit: Mango 14, Banana 6, Apple 9, Guava 5. How many children chose banana or guava?
hints: You need to put two groups from the table together.
Pick out only the numbers for banana and guava. They are 6 and 5.
Example: Rose 8, Lily 7, Lotus 4. The children who chose rose or lotus are 8 + 4 = 12.

stepByStep.text: Banana was chosen by 6 children and guava by 5 children.

misconceptions.A: This subtracts 5 from 6. The question asks for both groups together, so add them.
misconceptions.B: This adds mango and banana. The question asks about banana and guava.
misconceptions.C: This adds all four fruits. Only banana and guava are needed.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 6 children and 5 children make 11 children.

questionText: Six children got these marks in a spelling test: 14, 18, 9, 20, 12, 17. How many children got more than 15 marks?
hints: Here you count how many numbers in a list are bigger than a given number.
Go through the marks one at a time and tick each one that is bigger than 15. Start with 14: is it bigger than 15?
Example: Marks 6, 11, 8, 13, 5. The marks more than 10 are 11 and 13, so 2 children got more than 10.

stepByStep.text: 14, 9 and 12 are less than 15. The marks 18, 20 and 17 are more than 15.
That makes 3 children with more than 15 marks.

misconceptions.A: One of the marks above 15 has been missed. Check 18, 20 and 17 again.
misconceptions.B: Good checking! 18, 20 and 17 are the marks above 15, so the count is 3.
misconceptions.C: This also counts 14, but 14 is less than 15. Count only the marks bigger than 15.
misconceptions.D: This counts all six children. Count only the children whose marks are bigger than 15.

questionText: Each child in a class chose one favourite game: Cricket 13, Kho-kho 8, Football 7, Carrom 4. How many children are there in the class?
hints: Every child chose exactly one game, so the whole class is all the groups put together.
Add the four numbers. A good start is 13 + 7, which makes a round number.
Example: Tea 9, Milk 11, Juice 5. All together that is 9 + 11 + 5 = 25 people.

stepByStep.text: There are 32 children in the class.

misconceptions.A: This leaves out the 4 children who chose carrom. Add all four groups.
misconceptions.B: This counts the number of games. The question asks for the number of children, so add the four numbers.
misconceptions.C: That is right! 13 + 8 + 7 + 4 = 32.
misconceptions.D: The ones add up to more than 10 here, so a ten must be carried. Try adding 13 + 7 first, then 8 + 4.

questionText: In a tally chart, a bundle stands for 5 and a single stroke stands for 1. Which of these shows 23?
hints: Think about how many full fives fit into the number, and what is left over.
Count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20. How many fives is that, and how many more do you need to reach 23?
Example: To show 12, count in fives: 5, 10. That is 2 bundles, and 12 - 10 = 2 single strokes.

stepByStep.text: So 23 is shown by 4 bundles and 3 strokes.

misconceptions.A: This copies the digits 2 and 3 of the number 23. But 2 bundles are only 10, so this shows 13.
misconceptions.B: Lovely! 4 bundles make 20 and 3 strokes make 23.
misconceptions.C: 5 bundles are already 25, which is more than 23. Use fewer bundles.
misconceptions.D: 3 bundles make 15, and 4 more strokes make 19. Count in fives until you are close to 23.

questionText: In a pictograph, each picture of a sun stands for 2 sunny days. January has 5 pictures, February has 8 pictures, March has 6 pictures and April has 9 pictures. Which month had 16 sunny days?
hints: Each picture stands for more than one day, so the number of pictures is not the number of days.
Work out how many pictures are needed to show 16 days when each picture stands for 2 days.
Example: Each picture stands for 5 pens. To show 20 pens you need 20 divided by 5 = 4 pictures, so look for the row with 4 pictures.

stepByStep.text: Each picture stands for 2 days, so 16 days need 8 pictures.
The month with 8 pictures is February.

misconceptions.A: January has 5 pictures, which stand for 10 sunny days. Find the month with 8 pictures.
misconceptions.B: March has 6 pictures, which stand for 12 sunny days. Find the month with 8 pictures.
misconceptions.C: April has 9 pictures, which stand for 18 sunny days. That is a little too many.
misconceptions.D: Yes! February has 8 pictures and 8 x 2 = 16 sunny days.

questionText: The heights of five plants in centimetres are: Rose 34, Tulsi 28, Neem 41, Mint 19, Lily 37. Which plant is the second tallest?
hints: Put the numbers in order from biggest to smallest, then pick the one in second place.
Find the tallest plant first. Which height is the biggest of 34, 28, 41, 19 and 37?
Example: Asha 22, Bina 30, Charu 26. From biggest to smallest: 30, 26, 22. The second biggest is 26, so Charu is second tallest.

stepByStep.text: From biggest to smallest the heights are 41, 37, 34, 28, 19.
The tallest is 41 (Neem). The next is 37.
37 cm is the height of Lily, so the second tallest plant is Lily.

misconceptions.A: Super! Neem is tallest at 41 cm, and Lily comes next at 37 cm.
misconceptions.B: Neem is the tallest plant. The question asks for the second tallest, the one just below it.
misconceptions.C: Rose is 34 cm, which is third. One plant is taller than Rose but shorter than Neem.
misconceptions.D: Tulsi is second in the list, but the list is not in order of height. Arrange the heights from biggest to smallest first.

questionText: The side of a bar graph is marked 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. The top of Tuesday's bar is exactly halfway between the marks 20 and 30. What number does Tuesday's bar show?
hints: When a bar ends between two marks, its value is between those two numbers.
Find the number that is exactly in the middle of 20 and 30. How far apart are 20 and 30?
Example: A bar ends halfway between 40 and 60. The marks are 20 apart, half of 20 is 10, and 40 + 10 = 50.

misconceptions.A: 20 is the mark below the top of the bar. The bar goes up beyond 20, halfway to 30.
misconceptions.B: 30 is the mark above the top of the bar. The bar stops halfway before it reaches 30.
misconceptions.C: That is right! 25 is exactly in the middle of 20 and 30.
misconceptions.D: This adds 20 and 30. The bar ends between the two marks, so find the number in the middle of them.

questionText: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 3 kites. Ravi's row has 5 pictures and Meena's row has 8 pictures. How many more kites does Meena have than Ravi?
hints: This is a pictograph comparison. Remember that each picture stands for more than one kite.
Find how many more pictures Meena has than Ravi: 8 - 5.
Example: Each picture stands for 4 balls. Amit has 6 pictures and Sunil has 4 pictures. Amit has 2 more pictures, and 2 x 4 = 8 more balls.

stepByStep.text: Meena has 3 more pictures than Ravi.
Meena has 9 more kites than Ravi.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 3 extra pictures, each worth 3 kites, make 9 kites.
misconceptions.B: This is how many more pictures Meena has. Each picture stands for 3 kites, so multiply by 3.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of kites Meena has. The question asks how many more she has than Ravi.
misconceptions.D: This adds Ravi's 15 kites and Meena's 24 kites. To find how many more, subtract.

questionText: In a pictograph of library books, each picture stands for 5 books. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday has 6 pictures and Wednesday has 3 pictures. How many books were borrowed on the three days altogether?
hints: Find the total number of pictures, then change pictures into books.
Add the pictures for the three days: 4 + 6 + 3.
Example: Each picture stands for 2 pens. Three rows have 3, 5 and 4 pictures. That is 12 pictures, and 12 x 2 = 24 pens.

stepByStep.text: Add the pictures for the three days.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of pictures. Each picture stands for 5 books, so multiply by 5.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 13 pictures stand for 13 x 5 = 65 books.
misconceptions.C: This adds 5 to the 13 pictures. Each of the 13 pictures stands for 5 books, so multiply.
misconceptions.D: One picture has been missed. There are 4 + 6 + 3 = 13 pictures in all, not 12.

questionText: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 6 eggs. A farmer's chart has 5 pictures for Monday and 3 pictures for Tuesday. He packs all these eggs in boxes of 12. How many boxes does he fill?
hints: There are two parts here: first find the number of eggs, then share them into boxes.
Find the total number of pictures for the two days, then multiply by 6 to get the eggs.
Example: Each picture stands for 4 buns. There are 6 pictures, so 24 buns. Packed in bags of 8, that is 24 divided by 8 = 3 bags.

stepByStep.text: Put the eggs in boxes of 12.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of pictures. Change the pictures into eggs, then into boxes of 12.
misconceptions.B: This is the number of eggs. The question asks how many boxes of 12 they fill.
misconceptions.C: Great work! 48 eggs fill 4 boxes of 12.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts the pictures. Both days' eggs are packed, so add the pictures first.

questionText: A sweet shop sold 60 laddoos in four days. The table shows: Mon 12, Tue 18, Thu 14, but the number for Wednesday is smudged. How many laddoos were sold on Wednesday?
hints: You know the whole and three of its four parts. Think about how to find the missing part.
Add the three numbers you can read: 12 + 18 + 14.
Example: Total 50, and three days show 10, 15 and 5. These add to 30, so the missing day is 50 - 30 = 20.

stepByStep.text: Take this away from the total.

misconceptions.A: This is the total for the three known days. Take it away from 60 to find Wednesday.
misconceptions.B: This shares 60 equally among four days. The days are not equal, so subtract the known days from the total.
misconceptions.C: This adds the three days to 60. The 60 already includes them, so subtract.

questionText: Tickets sold at a mela: on Saturday, 20 adult tickets and 35 child tickets; on Sunday, 28 adult tickets and 30 child tickets. How many more tickets were sold on Sunday than on Saturday?
hints: Each day has two kinds of ticket. Find each day's total before you compare.
Add the adult and child tickets for Saturday: 20 + 35.
Example: Day 1 has 10 and 12 tickets, total 22. Day 2 has 15 and 14 tickets, total 29. Day 2 sold 29 - 22 = 7 more.

stepByStep.text: 3 more tickets were sold on Sunday.

misconceptions.A: That is right! Sunday's 58 tickets are 3 more than Saturday's 55.
misconceptions.B: This compares only the adult tickets. Child tickets count too, so find each day's total.
misconceptions.C: This compares only the child tickets. Add adult and child tickets for each day first.
misconceptions.D: This adds all the tickets of both days. To find how many more, subtract Saturday's total from Sunday's.

questionText: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 4 children and Monday's row has 6 pictures. The chart is drawn again with each picture standing for 8 children. How many pictures will Monday's row have now?
hints: The number of children stays the same. Only the value of each picture changes.
Find how many children Monday's row shows: 6 pictures of 4 children each.
Example: 10 pictures of 2 pens each show 20 pens. If each picture stands for 5 pens, you need 20 divided by 5 = 4 pictures.

stepByStep.text: Each new picture stands for 8 children.

misconceptions.A: This doubles the pictures. When each picture stands for more children, fewer pictures are needed.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 24 children need only 3 pictures of 8.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of children. The question asks how many pictures of 8 children are needed.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 6 by 8. Find the number of children first, then divide by 8.

questionText: In a pictograph, a full picture stands for 10 coconuts and a half picture stands for 5 coconuts. Monday's row has 3 full pictures and 1 half picture. Tuesday's row has 2 full pictures. How many coconuts were sold on the two days together?
hints: Work out each day's coconuts, counting full pictures and half pictures separately.
For Monday, find 3 full pictures of 10 and then add 5 for the half picture.
Example: A full picture is 4 and a half picture is 2. A row with 2 full pictures and 1 half picture shows 8 + 2 = 10.

stepByStep.text: Monday: 3 full pictures and a half picture.
55 coconuts were sold on the two days.

misconceptions.A: This leaves out the half picture. A half picture stands for 5 coconuts, so add 5.
misconceptions.B: This counts the half picture as a full one. A half picture stands for only 5 coconuts.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Monday's 35 and Tuesday's 20 make 55.
misconceptions.D: This is how many more were sold on Monday. The question asks for both days together.

questionText: A tally chart of birds uses bundles of 5 and single strokes. Crows: 2 bundles and 3 strokes. Sparrows: 3 bundles and 1 stroke. Pigeons: 1 bundle and 4 strokes. How many birds were counted in all?
hints: Change each tally row into a number, then add the rows.
Start with crows: 2 bundles are 10, and 3 strokes more.
Example: Row one has 1 bundle and 2 strokes, which is 7. Row two has 2 bundles and 1 stroke, which is 11. Together 7 + 11 = 18.

misconceptions.A: This counts every bundle as 1. Each bundle stands for 5 birds.
misconceptions.B: This counts the bundles but leaves out the single strokes. Add the 3, 1 and 4 strokes too.
misconceptions.C: This adds only the single strokes. The 6 bundles stand for 30 more birds.

questionText: A bar graph shows kites sold: Mon 14, Tue 9, Wed 17, Thu 11. Friday's bar is twice as tall as Tuesday's bar. How many kites were sold on the five days altogether?
hints: One value is not given directly. Find it from the clue, then add all five days.
Find Friday's number first. It is twice Tuesday's number, which is 9.
Example: Mon 5, Tue 8, and Wednesday is twice Monday. Wednesday is 10, and the total is 5 + 8 + 10 = 23.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Four days give 51, Friday gives 18, and 51 + 18 = 69.
misconceptions.B: This is the total for Monday to Thursday. Friday's kites must be added too.
misconceptions.C: This adds 2 for Friday. Twice as tall means 2 times Tuesday's 9, which is 18.
misconceptions.D: This takes Friday the same as Tuesday. Friday's bar is twice as tall, so it shows 18.

questionText: 40 children each chose one favourite game. Cricket was chosen by 16, football by 10 and badminton by 8. All the others chose kabaddi. How many children chose kabaddi?
hints: The whole group is known. The children who are left over after three games chose the fourth game.
Add the children who chose cricket, football and badminton: 16 + 10 + 8.
Example: 30 children; 12 chose red and 9 chose blue, the rest chose green. 12 + 9 = 21, so green got 30 - 21 = 9.

stepByStep.text: Take this away from all the children.

misconceptions.A: This is the number who chose the other three games. Take it away from 40.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 40 - 34 = 6.
misconceptions.C: This takes away cricket and football only. Badminton's 8 children must be taken away too.
misconceptions.D: This takes away cricket and badminton only. Football's 10 children must be taken away too.

questionText: Meera read 12 pages on Monday, 0 pages on Tuesday, 9 pages on Wednesday and 15 pages on Thursday. What is the average number of pages she read per day over these four days?
hints: An average shares the total equally over all the days, even a day when nothing was read.
Add the pages for all four days: 12 + 0 + 9 + 15.
Example: Goals in three matches are 4, 0 and 2. The total is 6, and 6 divided by 3 matches = 2 goals per match.

stepByStep.text: There are 4 days, and Tuesday counts as a day too.
The average is 9 pages per day.

misconceptions.A: This divides by 3 and leaves Tuesday out. Tuesday is still one of the four days, so divide by 4.
misconceptions.B: This is the total number of pages. For the average, share the total equally among the 4 days.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 36 pages shared over 4 days is 9 pages per day.
misconceptions.D: This is the biggest number in the list. The average is the total shared equally over the 4 days.

questionText: A bar graph shows cups of tea sold: Mon 22, Tue 17, Wed 25, Thu 19. Which list puts the days in order from the shortest bar to the tallest bar?
hints: The shortest bar shows the smallest number and the tallest bar shows the biggest number.
Find the smallest of 22, 17, 25 and 19. That day comes first.
Example: Sun 8, Mon 5, Tue 9. From smallest to biggest the numbers are 5, 8, 9, so the order is Mon, Sun, Tue.

stepByStep.text: From smallest to biggest the numbers are 17, 19, 22, 25.
17 is Tuesday, 19 is Thursday, 22 is Monday and 25 is Wednesday.
The order from shortest to tallest is Tue, Thu, Mon, Wed.

misconceptions.A: This list goes from the tallest bar to the shortest. The question asks for shortest first.
misconceptions.B: Tuesday and Wednesday are in the right places, but Thursday's 19 is smaller than Monday's 22.
misconceptions.C: This is the order of the days in the week. Put them in order of their numbers instead.
misconceptions.D: Lovely! 17, 19, 22, 25 gives Tue, Thu, Mon, Wed.

questionText: A school has three clubs. Art: 9 girls and 6 boys. Music: 7 girls and 11 boys. Chess: 5 girls and 12 boys. Which club has the most children?
hints: Each club has girls and boys. Find each club's total before comparing.
Add the girls and boys in the Art club: 9 + 6.
Example: Team P has 4 girls and 9 boys, 13 in all. Team Q has 8 girls and 6 boys, 14 in all. Team Q has more children.

stepByStep.text: 18 is the biggest total, so the club with the most children is Music.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Music has 18 children, more than Art's 15 and Chess's 17.
misconceptions.B: Art has the most girls, but the question asks about all children. Add girls and boys for each club.
misconceptions.C: Chess has the most boys, but with its girls it has 17 children. One club has more.
misconceptions.D: The totals are 15, 18 and 17, so they are not equal. Find the biggest total.

questionText: Children chose their favourite fruit: Mango 18, Apple 9, Banana 12, Orange 6, Grapes 3. Which fruit was chosen by exactly twice as many children as orange?
hints: Twice as many means two times a number. Find that number, then look for it in the list.
Orange was chosen by 6 children. Work out 2 times 6.
Example: Tea 4, Milk 8, Juice 10. Twice as many as tea is 2 x 4 = 8, and that is milk.

stepByStep.text: 12 children chose banana, so the answer is Banana.

misconceptions.A: Mango's 18 is three times orange's 6. Twice 6 is 12.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 2 x 6 = 12, and 12 children chose banana.
misconceptions.C: Apple's 9 is 3 more than orange's 6, not twice as many. Twice 6 is 12.
misconceptions.D: Grapes' 3 is half of orange's 6. Twice as many means 2 times 6.

questionText: Hardik played 5 cricket matches. His average score was 32 runs per match. How many runs did he score in the 5 matches altogether?
hints: An average tells you what each match would have if the total were shared equally. Here you go back from the average to the total.
Think of every one of the 5 matches as having 32 runs.
Example: The average of 4 matches is 20 runs. The total is 4 x 20 = 80 runs.

stepByStep.text: The average is the total shared equally among the matches.
So the total is the average multiplied by the number of matches.

misconceptions.A: This adds 32 and 5. The total is 5 lots of 32, so multiply.
misconceptions.B: This subtracts 5 from 32. The total is 5 lots of 32, so multiply.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 5 matches of 32 runs make 160 runs.
misconceptions.D: This is 2 lots of 32. There are 5 matches, so find 5 lots of 32.

questionText: The rainfall in a town, in millimetres, was: Mon 6, Tue 10, Wed 4, Thu 12, Fri 8. On how many days was the rainfall more than the average for the five days?
hints: There are two jobs here: find the average first, then compare each day with it.
Add the five numbers and divide the total by 5 to get the average.
Example: Values 3, 9, 6. The average is 18 divided by 3 = 6. Only 9 is more than 6, so 1 value is above the average.

stepByStep.text: Compare each day with 8: only 10 and 12 are more than 8. Friday's 8 is equal to the average, not more.
The rainfall was more than the average on 2 days.

misconceptions.A: This also counts Friday. Friday's rainfall is equal to the average, and the question asks for more than the average.
misconceptions.B: This is the average itself. Now count the days whose rainfall is more than 8.
misconceptions.C: This counts every day that is different from the average. Count only the days above 8.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The average is 8, and only Tuesday and Thursday are above it.

questionText: Ananya's average mark in 4 tests was 18. After the 5th test, her average for all 5 tests became 20. How many marks did she get in the 5th test?
hints: An average multiplied by the number of tests gives the total. Compare the total before and after.
Find Ananya's total marks in the first 4 tests: 4 times 18.
Example: The average of 2 tests is 10, so the total is 20. After a 3rd test the average is 12, so the total is 36. The 3rd test was 36 - 20 = 16 marks.

stepByStep.text: She got 28 marks in the 5th test.

misconceptions.A: That is right! The total rose from 72 to 100, so the 5th test was 28.
misconceptions.B: A 5th mark of 20 would not pull an average of 18 all the way up to 20. Compare the two totals.
misconceptions.C: This adds 2 to 20. The 5th test has to lift the average of all five tests by 2, so compare the totals 72 and 100.
misconceptions.D: This adds the two averages. Change each average into a total first, then subtract.

questionText: A pictograph shows old newspapers collected by two classes. Class 4A has 7 pictures and Class 4B has 4 pictures. Each picture stands for the same number of newspapers. Class 4A collected 21 more newspapers than Class 4B. How many newspapers did Class 4A collect?
hints: The value of one picture is not given. Use the extra pictures and the extra newspapers to find it.
Class 4A has 7 - 4 = 3 more pictures. These 3 pictures stand for the 21 extra newspapers.
Example: Row one has 6 pictures, row two has 4, and row one shows 10 more. The 2 extra pictures stand for 10, so each picture is 5 and row one shows 6 x 5 = 30.

stepByStep.text: Class 4A has 7 pictures of 7 newspapers each.

misconceptions.A: This is what Class 4B collected: 4 pictures of 7. The question asks about Class 4A.
misconceptions.B: Great thinking! Each picture stands for 7, so 7 pictures stand for 49.

questionText: Class 4 has 42 children, and 23 of them are girls. 15 children come to school by bus, and 9 of these are girls. How many boys do NOT come by bus?
hints: Sort the children two ways: girls or boys, and bus or no bus. Find the boys' numbers step by step.

Example: 30 children, 18 girls, so 12 boys. 10 come by bus and 6 of them are girls, so 4 bus boys. Boys not by bus: 12 - 4 = 8.

stepByStep.text: Boys who do not come by bus.
13 boys do not come by bus.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of boys who do come by bus. Take them away from all the boys.
misconceptions.B: This is the number of girls who do not come by bus. The question asks about boys.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 19 boys in all, 6 by bus, so 13 not by bus.
misconceptions.D: This is the number of all the boys. Take away the 6 boys who come by bus.

questionText: Vikram found the average of five numbers to be 20. Then he saw that he had copied one number as 25 when it was really 15. What is the correct average?
hints: A slip in one number changes the total, and the change is shared among all five numbers.
Find the total Vikram used: 5 times 20.
Example: The average of 4 numbers is 10, so the total is 40. One number was written as 12 instead of 4, so the true total is 40 - 8 = 32 and the true average is 32 divided by 4 = 8.

stepByStep.text: The number was 10 too big, so take 10 off.
Share the correct total among the five numbers.

misconceptions.A: This makes the total bigger. The copied number was too big, so the correct total is smaller.
misconceptions.B: This takes the whole 10 away from the average. The 10 is shared among five numbers, so the average falls by only 2.
misconceptions.C: This is the number that was copied badly. The average comes from the corrected total, 90, divided by 5.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The total drops from 100 to 90, and 90 divided by 5 is 18.

questionText: A shop sold school bags: Mon 14, Tue 18, Wed 10. On Saturday it sold as many bags as on Monday and Tuesday together. On Sunday it sold half as many bags as on Saturday. How many bags did it sell on these five days altogether?
hints: Two of the five numbers are hidden in clues. Find them one at a time, then add everything.
Find Saturday's number first: add Monday's 14 and Tuesday's 18.
Example: Mon 4, Tue 6. Saturday equals both together, 10, and Sunday is half of that, 5. The total is 4 + 6 + 10 + 5 = 25.

misconceptions.B: This leaves out Sunday's 16 bags. Sunday is half of Saturday.
misconceptions.C: This leaves out Saturday's 32 bags. Saturday equals Monday and Tuesday together.
misconceptions.D: This takes Sunday the same as Saturday. Sunday is half of Saturday, so it is 16.

questionText: Four friends have 8, 14, 11 and 7 marbles. They share the marbles so that all four have the same number. How many marbles must the friend who had 14 give away?
hints: Sharing equally gives everyone the average. Find what each friend ends up with.
Add all the marbles: 8 + 14 + 11 + 7.
Example: Three friends have 1, 9 and 2 sweets. The total is 12, so each gets 12 divided by 3. The friend with 9 keeps that equal share and gives away the other 5 sweets.

stepByStep.text: That friend must give away 4 marbles.

misconceptions.A: This is how many marbles each friend ends up with. The question asks how many the friend with 14 gives away.
misconceptions.B: That is right! Each friend ends with 10, so the friend with 14 gives away 4.
misconceptions.C: This is the gap between 14 and 8. Find the equal share first, then see how far 14 is above it.
misconceptions.D: This is the gap between 14 and 7. Find the equal share first, then see how far 14 is above it.

questionText: Riya and Kabir each drew a pictograph of their stamps. In Riya's chart each picture stands for 5 stamps and there are 12 pictures. In Kabir's chart each picture stands for 8 stamps and there are 7 pictures. Who has more stamps, and by how many?
hints: The two charts use different values for a picture, so you cannot compare the pictures directly.
Change Riya's pictures into stamps: 12 pictures of 5 stamps each.
Example: Chart one has 6 pictures of 2, which is 12. Chart two has 3 pictures of 5, which is 15. Chart two shows 15 - 12 = 3 more.

misconceptions.A: The gap of 4 is right, but check who has more: Riya has 60 stamps and Kabir has 56.
misconceptions.B: This compares the numbers of pictures, 12 and 7. Change the pictures into stamps first.
misconceptions.C: Super! Riya's 60 stamps are 4 more than Kabir's 56.
misconceptions.D: This compares the values of one picture, 8 and 5. Find each child's total stamps first.

questionText: In a pictograph, 🍎 = 5 apples. If Monday shows 🍎🍎🍎, how many apples were sold?
questionLatex: In a pictograph, 🍎 = 5 apples. If Monday shows 🍎🍎🍎, how many apples were sold?
hints: This is a pictograph question. Each picture stands for more than one thing, so look at the key first.
Count how many apple pictures Monday shows. Each one stands for 5 apples.
A similar example: one star picture stands for 4 books and Tuesday shows 6 stars. 6 × 4 = 24 books.

stepByStep.text: The key says each picture stands for 5 apples.

misconceptions.A: This is 3 + 5. Each of the 3 pictures stands for 5 apples, so multiply instead of adding.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 3 pictures of 5 apples each make 3 × 5 = 15 apples.

questionText: In a bar graph, the tallest bar represents:
questionLatex: In a bar graph, the tallest bar represents:
hints: This question is about reading a bar graph. Think about what the height of a bar tells you.
Imagine a bar graph of marks. A child with more marks gets a taller bar. So what does the tallest bar show?
A similar example: in a bar graph of rainfall, the shortest bar belongs to the month with the least rain. The height of a bar always matches the size of its value.

stepByStep.text: In a bar graph, the height of each bar shows how big its value is.
A bigger value gets a taller bar.
So the tallest bar represents the largest value.

misconceptions.A: The average is found by adding all the values and sharing equally. It is not shown by the tallest bar. Think about what a taller bar means.
misconceptions.B: A value of zero would have no bar at all. A tall bar means a big value.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The taller the bar, the larger the value.
misconceptions.D: The smallest value has the shortest bar. Think about what the tallest one means.

questionText: The mean of 12, 15, 18, 21, 24 is:
hints: This asks for the mean, which is another word for average. It is the fair share if the total were split equally.
First add all five numbers together. Then think about how many numbers there are.
A similar example: the mean of 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12. Add them: 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12 = 40. There are 5 numbers, so 40 ÷ 5 = 8. The mean is 8.

stepByStep.text: There are 5 numbers, so divide the total by 5.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The total is 90 and 90 ÷ 5 = 18.
misconceptions.B: 15 is one of the numbers, but not the fair share. Add all five numbers and divide by 5.
misconceptions.C: Check your total. The five numbers add up to 90, and then you divide by 5.
misconceptions.D: 90 is the total of the numbers. To get the mean, divide the total by how many numbers there are.

questionText: The mode of 3, 5, 7, 5, 9, 5, 2 is:
hints: This asks for the mode. The mode is the number that appears most often in a list.
Go through the list and count how many times each number appears. A tally can help.
A similar example: in 4, 8, 6, 8, 1, 8, 6 the number 8 appears three times and 6 appears twice. Nothing appears more often than 8, so the mode is 8.

stepByStep.text: Count how many times each number appears in 3, 5, 7, 5, 9, 5, 2.
5 appears 3 times. Every other number appears only once.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 5 appears three times, more than any other number.
misconceptions.B: 9 is the biggest number, but the mode is the one that appears most often. Count each number.
misconceptions.C: 7 appears only once. Look for the number that shows up the most times.
misconceptions.D: 3 is the first number in the list, but it appears only once. Look for the number that shows up the most.

questionText: The range of 14, 8, 22, 5, 17 is:
hints: This asks for the range. The range tells you how far apart the biggest and smallest numbers are.
Find the biggest number and the smallest number in the list. You will need both.
A similar example: the range of 6, 19, 11, 3 and 15. The biggest is 19 and the smallest is 3. 19 − 3 = 16, so the range is 16.

stepByStep.text: The biggest number is 22 and the smallest is 5.
Subtract the smallest from the biggest.

misconceptions.A: This is 22 + 5. For the range, subtract the smallest from the biggest instead of adding.
misconceptions.B: 14 is the first number in the list. The range is the biggest number minus the smallest.
misconceptions.C: 5 is the smallest number. The range is how far it is from the biggest number.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 22 − 5 = 17, so the range is 17.

questionText: In a pictograph, ☺ = 10 students. ☺☺½ represents:
hints: This is a pictograph question with a half picture. A half picture stands for half of what a full one stands for.
Count the full pictures first and work out what they stand for. Then find what half a picture is worth.
A similar example: one picture stands for 8 toys, and a row shows 3 full pictures and a half. 3 × 8 = 24, and half of 8 is 4. 24 + 4 = 28 toys.

stepByStep.text: Each full picture stands for 10 students. There are 2 full pictures.
The half picture stands for half of 10.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Two full pictures make 20 and the half makes 5 more, so 25.
misconceptions.B: This counts one full picture and a half. There are two full pictures before the half.
misconceptions.C: This counts only the two full pictures. The half picture stands for 5 more students.
misconceptions.D: This counts the half picture as a full one. Half a picture stands for 5 students, not 10.

questionText: Bar A = 45, Bar B = 30. Difference:
hints: This asks for the difference between two bars. Difference means how much more one is than the other.
To find a difference, take the smaller value away from the bigger one.
A similar example: one bar shows 62 and another shows 40. 62 − 40 = 22, so the difference is 22.

stepByStep.text: Difference means subtract the smaller value from the bigger one.
Bar A is 45 and Bar B is 30.

misconceptions.A: Check your subtraction. 45 − 30 leaves 1 ten and 5 ones.
misconceptions.B: This is 45 + 30. Difference means subtract, not add.
misconceptions.C: This is 45 ÷ 30. Difference means subtract the smaller from the bigger.

questionText: If you toss a coin, getting a head is:
questionLatex: If you toss a coin, getting a head is:
hints: This is about chance. Think about all the things that can happen when you toss a coin.
A coin has two sides, heads and tails. Is one side more likely to land face up than the other?
A similar example: a bag has 5 red balls and 5 blue balls. Each colour has the same number of balls, so picking red has the same chance as picking blue.

stepByStep.text: A coin has two sides: heads and tails.
Both sides have the same chance of landing face up.
So getting a head is equally likely as tails.

misconceptions.A: Certain means it must happen every time. A coin can also land on tails. Compare the chances of the two sides.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Heads and tails each have the same chance.
misconceptions.C: Impossible means it can never happen. A coin does land on heads sometimes. Compare the chances of the two sides.
misconceptions.D: Likely means it happens more often than not. Heads does not come up more often than tails. The two sides have the same chance.

questionText: A table shows: Mon=12, Tue=15, Wed=18, Thu=10, Fri=20. Total:
questionLatex: A table shows: Mon=12, Tue=15, Wed=18, Thu=10, Fri=20. Total:
hints: This asks for a total from a table. Total means add all the values together.
Add the numbers a few at a time. Look for pairs that make easy tens, like 12 and 18.
A similar example: Mon = 11, Tue = 14, Wed = 9, Thu = 16. Pair them up: 11 + 9 = 20 and 14 + 16 = 30. Then 20 + 30 = 50 in total.

misconceptions.A: This is 10 too few. Check that all five days are added in.

misconceptions.D: This is 5 too few. Check the ones digits when you add the 15.

questionText: Average of 5 numbers is 20. Four numbers are 15, 22, 18, 25. Find the 5th.
questionLatex: Average of 5 numbers is 20. Four numbers are 15, 22, 18, 25. Find the 5th.
hints: This is an average problem worked backwards. If you know the average and how many numbers there are, you can find their total.
First find the total of all five numbers. Multiply the average by how many numbers there are.
A similar example: the average of 4 numbers is 10, and three of them are 8, 12 and 9. The total must be 4 × 10 = 40. The three known numbers add up to 29. 40 − 29 = 11, so the fourth number is 11.

stepByStep.text: The total of all 5 numbers is the average times 5.
Add the four numbers you know.
The fifth number is what is left.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The total must be 100, the four known numbers make 80, and 100 − 80 = 20.
misconceptions.B: 25 is one of the four numbers already given. Find the total of all five, then take away the four you know.
misconceptions.C: 80 is the sum of the four known numbers. Take it away from the total of all five.
misconceptions.D: 100 is the total of all five numbers. Take away the four you know to find the fifth.

questionText: An event that will definitely happen is called:
questionLatex: An event that will definitely happen is called:
hints: This is about the words we use for chance. Each word tells how sure we are that something will happen.
Think of something that must happen, like the sun rising tomorrow. Which word says there is no doubt at all?
A similar example: picking a green ball from a bag that has only red balls can never happen. An event that can never happen is called impossible.

stepByStep.text: Some events may or may not happen. Others can never happen.
An event that will definitely happen has no doubt about it.
Such an event is called certain.

misconceptions.A: Uncertain means we are not sure. The question says the event will definitely happen.
misconceptions.B: Impossible means it can never happen. That is the opposite of what the question asks.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Certain means it will definitely happen.
misconceptions.D: Unlikely means it probably will not happen. Look for the word that means it will surely happen.

questionText: In a pie chart, if 'Cricket' takes up 1/4 of the circle, the angle is:

hints: This is about a pie chart. A full circle has 360 degrees at its centre, and each slice takes a share of that.
The slice is one quarter of the circle. So you need one quarter of the full turn of 360 degrees.
A similar example: a slice that takes up 1/6 of the circle. 360 ÷ 6 = 60, so its angle is 60 degrees.

misconceptions.A: 45° is one eighth of the circle. One quarter is 360 ÷ 4.
misconceptions.B: 180° is half of the circle. One quarter is smaller than that.
misconceptions.C: 120° is one third of the circle. For one quarter, divide 360 by 4.
misconceptions.D: Yes! One quarter of 360° is 90°.

questionText: Find the median of: 7, 3, 9, 5, 11.

A similar example: the median of 8, 2, 6, 12 and 4. In order they are 2, 4, 6, 8, 12. The middle one is 6, so the median is 6.

stepByStep.text: There are 5 numbers, so the middle one is the third.

misconceptions.A: 3 is the smallest number. The median is the middle number after putting them in order.
misconceptions.B: 5 is the second number in order. Count to the middle of the five numbers.
misconceptions.C: 9 is in the middle of the list as it is written. Put the numbers in order first, then find the middle.
misconceptions.D: Yes! In order the numbers are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 7 is in the middle.

questionText: 36 books need to be shown. If each symbol = 6 books, how many symbols?
questionLatex: 36 books need to be shown. If each symbol = 6 books, how many symbols?
hints: This is a pictograph question worked backwards. You know the total and what one symbol stands for, and you need the number of symbols.
Think of putting the 36 books into equal groups. Each group is one symbol.
A similar example: 56 pencils are shown and each symbol stands for 8 pencils. 56 ÷ 8 = 7, so 7 symbols are needed.

stepByStep.text: Each symbol stands for 6 books. Share 36 books into groups of 6.

misconceptions.A: This is 36 − 6. You need to find how many groups of 6 fit into 36, so divide.
misconceptions.B: This is 36 × 6. The symbols group the books, so divide instead of multiplying.
misconceptions.C: 5 symbols show only 5 × 6 = 30 books. You need enough symbols for all 36.

questionText: A bar graph has scale: 1 cm = 20 students. A bar is 3.5 cm tall. Students:
questionLatex: A bar graph has scale: 1 cm = 20 students. A bar is 3.5 cm tall. Students:

A similar example: the scale is 1 cm = 10 students and a bar is 4.5 cm tall. 4 cm stands for 4 × 10 = 40 students, and half a centimetre stands for 5. 40 + 5 = 45 students.

stepByStep.text: Each centimetre stands for 20 students. Start with the 3 whole centimetres.
Half a centimetre stands for half of 20.

misconceptions.C: This is 3.5 × 10. The scale says each centimetre stands for 20 students.
misconceptions.D: This counts only the 3 whole centimetres. The extra half centimetre stands for 10 more students.

questionText: Rolling a 7 on a standard die (1-6) is:
questionLatex: Rolling a 7 on a standard die (1-6) is:
hints: This is about chance. Think about which numbers a die can show.
List the numbers on the faces of a standard die. Is 7 one of them?

stepByStep.text: A standard die has six faces showing 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
There is no face with 7 on it, so a 7 can never come up.

misconceptions.B: Certain means it happens every time. Check which numbers are on a die.
misconceptions.C: Unlikely means it can happen, but not often. Check whether a die has a 7 at all.

questionText: Average of 4 numbers is 25. Three numbers are 20, 30, 22. Find the fourth.
questionLatex: Average of 4 numbers is 25. Three numbers are 20, 30, 22. Find the fourth.
hints: This is an average problem worked backwards. The average and the count of numbers together tell you the total.
First find the total of all four numbers. Multiply the average by how many numbers there are.
A similar example: the average of 3 numbers is 12, and two of them are 9 and 13. The total must be 3 × 12 = 36. The two known numbers add up to 22. 36 − 22 = 14, so the third number is 14.

stepByStep.text: The total of all 4 numbers is the average times 4.
Add the three numbers you know.
The fourth number is what is left.

misconceptions.A: 25 is the average, not the missing number. Find the total of all four, then take away the three you know.

misconceptions.C: Yes! The total must be 100, the three known numbers make 72, and 100 − 72 = 28.
misconceptions.D: Check the total first. Four numbers with an average of 25 add up to 4 × 25 = 100. Then take away 72.
